name: Dejerine-Sottas disease (CMT3)
aliases: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type III

clinicalPearls: Severe, early-onset demyelinating hereditary neuropathy presenting in infancy or early childhood, historically labelled CMT3
Caused by variants in the same genes that cause CMT1, most often PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 or PRX, usually as de novo dominant or recessive changes
Children show delayed motor milestones, marked hypotonia, distal and sometimes proximal weakness, and prominent sensory loss with sensory ataxia
Peripheral nerves may be palpably hypertrophied owing to repeated demyelination and remyelination
Nerve conduction studies reveal extremely slow motor conduction velocities, among the slowest seen in any neuropathy
Skeletal deformities such as scoliosis and severe pes cavus are common because of the early and severe muscle imbalance
Diagnosis rests on severe demyelinating electrophysiology with genetic confirmation, viewing the condition as the severe end of the CMT1 spectrum
reference.pathophysiology: Dejerine-Sottas disease represents the severe end of the hereditary demyelinating neuropathy spectrum, arising from variants in peripheral myelin genes such as PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 and PRX. These variants profoundly disrupt Schwann cell myelination from early development, producing marked hypomyelination and repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination with abundant onion-bulb formation and nerve hypertrophy. The severe and diffuse myelin failure causes profound slowing of conduction and early secondary axonal loss, accounting for the early-onset weakness, sensory ataxia and disability. Many cases result from de novo dominant variants, so a negative family history is common.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy of childhood
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies demonstrating profoundly slow velocities
Sequencing of PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 and PRX or a broad hereditary neuropathy panel
Sural nerve biopsy showing hypomyelination and onion bulbs in selected cases
Spinal imaging and orthopaedic assessment for scoliosis and foot deformity
Exclusion of acquired inflammatory neuropathy of childhood
Developmental and multidisciplinary assessment given early-onset disability
redFlags: Respiratory compromise from severe early neuromuscular weakness
Subacute deterioration suggesting a treatable inflammatory neuropathy
Feeding or bulbar difficulty in an affected infant
reference.prognosis: Course is severe with early and substantial disability; many affected children have limited independent ambulation, although the degree varies with the specific gene and variant. Respiratory and skeletal complications may affect long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Excluding a genetic cause because there is no family history, when many cases are de novo
Mistaking severe inherited demyelination for acquired inflammatory neuropathy, or vice versa
Overlooking nerve hypertrophy as a diagnostic clue
Neglecting orthopaedic and respiratory surveillance in a severely affected child
references: GeneReviews: Charcot-Marie-Tooth Neuropathy Type 1 and Related Disorders
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Supportive, multidisciplinary care as there is no disease-specific pharmacotherapy, centred on physiotherapy to maintain mobility and prevent contractures
Orthotic and mobility support with ankle-foot orthoses, custom footwear and wheelchairs for progressive distal and proximal weakness and sensory ataxia
Orthopaedic surgical management of severe pes cavus and scoliosis arising from early muscle imbalance
Surveillance and support of respiratory function, which may determine long-term outcome
Neuropathic pain management with neuropathic agents, and avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular, rehabilitation and developmental support given early-onset disability
Genetic counselling and molecular confirmation across PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 and PRX with family testing, recognising frequent de novo dominant variants
